While this position required additional education over my BFA, I would never have gotten to where I am without it as an undergraduate degree of some stripe.

When interviewing for new hires, I look at college degrees quite differently than many people would assume. What one majors in is rarely of consequence, as college degrees show more that someone can handle the challenge of coursework, can think on their feet and persevere.

When going through job applications one of the very -first- things that tends to happen is that any resumes from people without college degrees go straight to the trash. When you get dozens of applications for a single position, it's one of the easiest ways to weed out your least qualified applicants. Naturally, this won't be true of every jobs. I have known employers who would do the opposite and get rid of college graduates because they were overqualified for the job and wouldn't stay long, but to be honest, most of those positions either came with a paper hat or a broom.

In the library, I run the Youth Services department, and I handle kids from birth through 18 (Early 20's too, really)

My time in art school proves very helpful in everything from the graphic design of our webpage and the fliers and signs I make within the library, to creating friendly and welcoming artwork and design choices within the children's area that make it a very inviting place for parents and kids. My library is one of the most successful in the state, we bring thousands of kids in for library programs every month. I wouldn't be such a success without what I learned in art school.

It would also be useful in a number of other areas of business, from knowing how to use color to influence people, designing slick graphics for proposals and reports, to coming up with an interesting and memorable business card just to name a few possibilities. A college education teaches you skills, where and how you use them is up to you. If you just look at time in college as straight career training, you're not getting very much out of your time there.

College education isn't just about cramming facts into brains, but is about developing the skills for critical thought and analysis on one's own. Just because someone doesn't get a job in the field of their major does not make for a wasted education, at all.

I'll also point out that in my parent's day, it was entirely possible for someone to work over the summer, save SOME of what they earned, and be able to pay college tuition with that money. That's pretty much impossible these days, we're saddling people with DECADES of debt for their education in ways that we never used to.

The US is falling behind in many of the STEM fields, and with technology increasingly taking over everything from communication to manufacturing, we need a labor force well stocked in technology skills.
